Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody shares what’s stressing them. Stress from money, home or racism happens to people; it isn’t a sign they cope badly. If something heavy comes up, let a counselor know that day.

Every student in the room

Keep the movement optional, and when the Jack and Lena cards come up, say plainly that stress from money, home, or racism is something that happens to people, not a sign they cope badly.

Ask which they notice first before something big. Butterflies read as “something’s wrong” tend to spiral; read as “I’m getting ready,” they settle.

Sapolsky’s zebra: the stress response is built for short bursts. Ask: what’s your recovery after a hard day? Recovery is part of the deal, not a reward for finishing.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain what the stress response does for them, use one way to read a racing heart as fuel, and tell the difference between a stress signal that settles and stress that stays stuck on. Nobody is asked to share what's stressing them or how much.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 2 minFeel it
  2. 3 minEvery feeling has a job
  3. 2 minSignal, effort, recovery
  4. 3 minThe research, and stuck on
  5. 3 minYour recovery: turn and talk, share out
  6. 5 minSignal or stuck on? Mia, Jack, Sam, Lena
  7. 2 minEvery student, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Feel it, every feeling has a job, and two of the signal-or-stuck-on cards.

Before you teach
Lead with the good news, and keep it honest.

Stress is necessary and the research backs that up: short bursts help focus and performance, and reading a racing heart as "getting ready" helps a little. Don't promise that a mindset makes stress harmless. The claim that stress only hurts people who believe it does goes beyond the evidence.

Some stress isn't a challenge.

For a student dealing with money worries, a parent's illness, conflict at home, or racism, "stress is good for you" can land as "your problem is how you think about it." Say plainly that stress which stays on is a different thing, that it often comes from things students can't control, and that it's a reason to bring in adults, not to think harder.

Keep the cards invented.

Use the scenario cards, not students' own stories. If a student starts describing something heavy, thank them, keep it brief in the group, and follow up privately.

Watch for stuck on.

Weeks of poor sleep, frequent headaches or stomachaches, pulling away, or using substances to come down are worth a quiet check-in after advisory and a same-day note to a counselor if it sounds serious. Disclosures go to a counselor. No screening questions in the group.

Panic and anxiety disorders are their own thing.

Some students have panic attacks or an anxiety disorder, and "it's just a signal" won't be enough for them. Point them to The False Alarm and to a counselor.

Model it.

Name a time your own heart pounded before something that mattered, and what you told yourself. It gives students permission to notice their own.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Stress isn't spread evenly.

Students carrying racism, poverty, immigration worries, caregiving, or unsafe neighborhoods face more stress that stays on. Name chronic stress as something that happens to people, not a flaw in how they cope.

Families name it differently.

Some families say nerves, pressure, or nothing at all; in some homes stress shows up as stomachaches or headaches. Ask what students' families call it, and treat faith, music, food, family and community as real ways of coping.

Movement for every body.

The opening movement is optional. Offer clapping fast, tapping feet, a few deep fast breaths, or simply noticing your pulse. Students with heart conditions, injuries or disabilities can sit it out without explaining.

Bodies that react differently.

Students with anxiety, trauma histories, or sensory sensitivities may find focusing on heartbeat uncomfortable. Make noticing optional and keep eyes-open.

Neurodivergent students.

Students with ADHD or autism may feel stress signals more or less strongly, or read them later. There's no right way to feel it. Concrete cards help.

Language.

English learners can answer with a word in any language, a gesture, or a number from 1 to 10.

What the research says

In a 30-minute online lesson tested in several studies with thousands of high school and college students, learning that stress responses can fuel performance (together with a growth mindset) improved heart and blood vessel responses to a stress test, lowered daily cortisol, reduced anxiety, and improved academic outcomes.

Yeager et al., Nature, 2022

People told that a racing heart helps them perform showed a more efficient cardiovascular response under social stress and paid less attention to threat.

Jamieson, Nock & Mendes, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2012

Students told that arousal can help did better on GRE math practice and on the real GRE months later.

Jamieson et al., Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2010

Believing stress can be enhancing was linked to better health and work performance, and a short video shifting that belief changed how people responded to stress.

Crum, Salovey & Achor, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2013

Short-term stress responses protect and prepare the body; harm comes when they are turned on too often or fail to turn off (allostatic load).

McEwen, New England Journal of Medicine, 1998

Developmental scientists separate positive stress (brief, mild), tolerable stress (serious but buffered by supportive adults), and toxic stress (strong, frequent or prolonged without that support).

National Scientific Council on the Developing Child, Harvard, 2005/2014

Worry and rumination keep the stress response switched on long after the stressful event is over.

Brosschot, Gerin & Thayer, Journal of Psychosomatic Research, 2006

Discrimination and poverty act as chronic stressors with measurable effects on mental and physical health.

Williams, Journal of Health and Social Behavior, 2018; Evans & Kim, Child Development Perspectives, 2013
